notes.short: “Oh, Lord GOD”: Ezekiel cries out for his people
notes.about: As the slaughter he is shown in Jerusalem goes on, Ezekiel, left alone, falls facedown and cries out, “Oh, Lord GOD,” pleading that the remnant of Israel not be wholly destroyed. The cry bursts from dismay and pity for his people.

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.means: the prophet's dismay and pity for his people as judgment falls on them

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Ecphonesis, or Exclamation. Calvin says the prophet, as if astonished, exclaims with vehemence and breaks forth into a cry, his fall on his face showing human affection; Henry, that he cried out not in fear for himself but in compassion; Gardiner (Ellicott), that he falls on his face in consternation and pleads for the remnant.

cites.quote: So that Ecphonesis is an outburst of words, prompted by emotion, and is not used as though any reply were expected. ... “I fell upon my face, and cried, and said, Ah Lord God (Adonai Jehovah)!” etc.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Now as the Prophet fell upon his face, it was a testimony of the human affection … This is the reason why the Prophet lies on his face, as if astonished, and exclaims with vehemence, Alas! O Lord God … Since, therefore, the Prophet saw that city destroyed, he broke forth into a cry
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: he fell on his face, and cried, not in fear for himself (he was one of those that were marked), but in compassion to his fellow-creatures.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Now it is a city of the dead, and he is left standing alone in the midst of the dead. He falls upon his face in consternation, and pleads that “the residue of Israel” may not be utterly destroyed.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: “Like mother, like daughter” turned on Jerusalem
notes.about: The LORD says people will quote the proverb “Like mother, like daughter” about Jerusalem. Her mother is the Hittite of verse 3, one of the peoples of Canaan, and she has taken up their ways. Many read it as showing her sin was so open that all could see it and make a byword of it.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.means: Jerusalem is as sinful as the Canaanite peoples whose ways she took up

original.note: In Hebrew the proverb is only two words, ke'immah bittah.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, a proverb already in use. Calvin says the saying was in everyone's mouth and her crimes earned her shame on every tongue. Henry, Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) and Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) apply it to Jerusalem as the Canaanites' daughter, Fausset noting it is two Hebrew words; Gardiner (Ellicott) says her sin was notorious enough to call it forth.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such, p. 757
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such ... “Behold, every one that useth proverbs shall use this proverb against thee, saying: ‘As is the mother, so is her daughter.’ ”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: the crimes of the nation deserved that their infamy should fly abroad on the tongues of all ... There is no doubt that they used this saying at that period ... hence this proverb was in the mouth of every one. ... Thus the Prophet means that the nation was like their mother, since it differed in nothing from the Canaanites and the Hittites.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Those that use proverbs, as most people do, shall apply that proverb to Jerusalem, As is the mother, so is her daughter ... She is her mother's own child. The Jews are as like the Canaanites in temper and inclination as if they had been their own children.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This characteristic is expressed in the form of proverbial sayings. ... Her abominable life is so conspicuous, that it strikes every one, and furnishes occasion for proverbial sayings. ... The daughter is of course Jerusalem, as the representative of Israel. The mother is the Canaanitish race of Hittites and Amorites, whose immoral nature had been adopted by Israel
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The sin of the people had become so notorious as to attract general attention, and lead to the application of this proverb. The nativity of Israel described in Eze 16:3 is here in mind, and the proverb becomes equivalent to saying, these sins belong to every people living in Canaan; once practised by the Amorites and Hittites, they are now continued by the Israelites.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: the ellipsis gives the proverb (but two words in the Hebrew) epigrammatic brevity. Jerusalem proved herself a true daughter of the Hittite mother in sin
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Two eagles and a vine: a riddle God then explains
notes.about: God has Ezekiel pose a riddle: an eagle takes the top of a cedar; a low vine turns to a second eagle and will wither. Then he is to ask, “Do you not know what these things mean?” The first eagle is the king of Babylon, who took Jerusalem’s king; the vine is the king he set up, who turned to Egypt.

figure.name: Riddle
figure.words: A great eagle with great wings and long pinions
figure.means: the king of Babylon, who came to Jerusalem and carried off its king, as verse 12 explains; the second eagle is Egypt’s king

original.note: In Hebrew the verb and the noun share one root: chud chidah, to riddle a riddle.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Ezekiel 17:2-10 under Ænigma: Babylon’s king taking Jerusalem captive, told as a riddle of two eagles. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): a riddle for its deeper sense; the eagles are Nebuchadnezzar and Egypt’s king, the seed Zedekiah. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) and Calvin call it dark, allegorical speech of Judah’s judgment; Henry, a riddle whose eagle is Nebuchadnezzar.
notes.limit: The text calls it both a riddle and a parable, and some writers call it an allegory. Several writers say it was told darkly not to puzzle the hearers but to rouse and teach them, since its meaning is given at once.

cites.quote: gives a prophecy concerning the King of Babylon’s coming to Jerusalem, and leading it into captivity, under the Enigma of two Eagles.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The parable (mâshâl, corresponding exactly to the New Testament παραβολή) is called chīdhâh, a riddle, because of the deeper meaning lying beneath the parabolic shell. ... The great eagle in Eze 17:3 is the great King Nebuchadnezzar ... The seed of the land ... is King Zedekiah ... The other eagle mentioned in Eze 17:7 is the king of Egypt, according to Eze 17:15 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: JUDAH IS TO BE JUDGED FOR REVOLTING FROM BABYLON, WHICH HAD SET UP ZEDEKIAH INSTEAD OF JEHOIACHIN, TO EGYPT ... riddle--a continued allegory, expressed enigmatically, requiring more than common acumen and serious thought. ... Not like the ordinary riddle, designed to puzzle, but to instruct.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: the noun and the verb mutually answer to each other, hence any one may if he please render the Prophet’s words, by saying enigmatize an enigma: for the Prophet here speaks of allegorical language ... here the obscurity of the sentence has another meaning, namely, that the Jews should be waked up ... in this place God so denounces destruction upon the Israelites in an allegory
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The prophet is appointed to put forth a riddle to the house of Israel ... he is immediately to tell them the meaning of it. ... But he must deliver this message in a riddle or parable that they might take the more notice of it ... Nebuchadnezzar had some time ago carried off Jehoiachin ... This in the parable is represented by an eagle's cropping the top and tender branch of a cedar
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: God's own parable: Jerusalem as a pot on the fire
notes.about: God tells Ezekiel to speak a parable: a pot set on the fire, filled with the best pieces of meat and boiled. From verse 6 God explains it: the pot is the city of bloodshed, Jerusalem, put under siege that very day. The meat in it stands for the city's people.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Put the pot on the fire
figure.means: Jerusalem under siege, with its people shut inside like meat in a boiling pot

original.note: In Hebrew the word for parable is mashal, which can also mean a proverb.

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the verses are called a proverb or parable, the pot with its meat representing Jerusalem and its people, the fire, war. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) and Clarke explain the pot as the city, the meat as its people. Matthew Henry: Jerusalem in the siege is like a boiling pot. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the people will be as meat in a boiling caldron.
notes.limit: Writers also give meanings to the choice pieces and the bones. The note keeps to the main likeness.

cites.quote: The contents of these verses are called משׁל, a proverb or parable ... The pot with the pieces of flesh and the bones, which are to be boiled in it and boiled away, represents Jerusalem with its inhabitants. The fire, with which they are boiled, is the fire of war ... The choicest pieces of flesh and the pieces of bone denote the strongest and ablest portion of the population of the city.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The prophet indicates by the figure utter destruction. The caldron is the city, the fire is the surrounding army, the flesh and bones are the inhabitants shut in within the walls.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The pot was Jerusalem; the flesh, the inhabitants in general; every good piece, the thigh and the shoulder, King Zedekiah and his family; the bones, the soldiers; and the setting on the pot, the commencement of the siege.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The comparison made use of is that of a boiling pot ... He must give them a comment upon this sign. It is to be construed as a woe to the bloody city ... Jerusalem, during the siege, is like a pot boiling over the fire, all in a heat, all in a hurry.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: So far from the city proving an iron, caldron-like defense from the fire, it shall be as a caldron set on the fire, and the people as so many pieces of meat subjected to boiling heat.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)
